lead: AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam fix one weakness of plain gradient descent: one learning rate for every weight. They give each weight its own effective step size from the history of its gradients. Adam is the default in many deep-learning libraries. The idea is simple: large, noisy gradients get smaller updates; small, rare gradients get larger updates. You meet them whenever a network is trained with mini-batches.
prereq: You need: mini-batch updates and momentum from Chapter 2.

sections.h3: AdaGrad: per-weight sum of squared gradients

blocks.text: AdaGrad changes the step size for every weight separately. Let g<sub>t</sub> be the gradient of loss J with respect to weight w at step t. AdaGrad keeps a cumulative sum G<sub>t</sub>. Large past gradients make the denominator large, so the current step becomes smaller. Small, rare gradients keep the denominator small, so their step remains larger. This suits sparse features, like one-hot encoded words in text models, where many weights get zero gradient most of the time.

blocks.where: G<sub>t</sub> is the sum of squared gradients up to step t; G<sub>0</sub> is usually 0.

blocks.text: The update is w<sub>t+1</sub> = w<sub>t</sub> − η g<sub>t</sub> / (√G<sub>t</sub> + ε). η is the base learning rate; ε is a tiny constant, often 10⁻⁸, to avoid division by zero. The weakness is clear: G only grows. After many steps, √G becomes very large, so the update can become nearly zero before the loss is low.

sections.h3: RMSProp: a decaying average of squared gradients

blocks.text: RMSProp fixes AdaGrad's ever-growing denominator. It does not sum all past squared gradients. It keeps an exponentially weighted moving average, usually written E[g²]<sub>t</sub>. Old squared gradients decay by factor β, so the denominator can rise and fall.

blocks.where: E[g²]<sub>t</sub> is the moving estimate of squared gradient; β is decay rate, typically 0.9.

blocks.text: Update: w<sub>t+1</sub> = w<sub>t</sub> − η g<sub>t</sub> / (√E[g²]<sub>t</sub> + ε). A noisy burst raises E[g²], so the step shrinks. When gradients become small again, E[g²] falls and the step can grow. RMSProp has no momentum; it only rescales the gradient. It is often used for recurrent networks and tasks where the gradient scale changes over time.
Adam combines momentum with RMSProp-style adaptive scaling. It keeps two moving averages: m<sub>t</sub> for the gradient mean and v<sub>t</sub> for the squared gradient.

blocks.where: m<sub>t</sub> is the first moment estimate of the gradient.
v<sub>t</sub> is the second moment estimate.

blocks.text: At the start m and v are zero, so early estimates are biased low. Adam corrects the bias: m̂<sub>t</sub> = m<sub>t</sub> / (1−β₁<sup>t</sup>), v̂<sub>t</sub> = v<sub>t</sub> / (1−β₂<sup>t</sup>). Then w<sub>t+1</sub> = w<sub>t</sub> − η m̂<sub>t</sub> / (√v̂<sub>t</sub> + ε). Standard defaults are η=0.001, β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, ε=10⁻⁸. Adam is often the first optimizer to try because these defaults work across many deep networks.

figure.caption: On loss J=½w², start w=1, η=0.1. AdaGrad uses cumulative G; RMSProp uses β=0.9; Adam uses β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, ε=10⁻⁸. RMSProp has the smallest denominator, so it takes the biggest steps; Adam's first update matches AdaGrad, but by the second update Adam moves further than AdaGrad.
figure.aria: A weight-versus-iteration plot compares AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam on the same quadratic loss; the three algorithms reach different weights at iteration 2.

examples.question: Run two Adam updates for J(w)=½w², starting at w=1. Use η=0.1, β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, ε=10⁻⁸, and initialize m₀=0, v₀=0. Report m, v, m̂, v̂, and w after each step.
examples.check:
import math
w,eta,b1,b2,eps,m,v=1.,.1,.9,.999,1e-8,0.,0.
for t in (1,2):
    g=w;m=b1*m+(1-b1)*g;v=b2*v+(1-b2)*g*g;w=w-eta*(m/(1-b1**t))/(math.sqrt(v/(1-b2**t))+eps)
    if t==1:w1=w
    else:w2=w
print(round(w1,3));print(round(w2,3))

traps: Forgetting Adam bias correction makes early updates different; with standard defaults the first step is much larger than the base learning rate, not smaller.
Placing ε inside the square root. It is added after: √v̂ + ε, not √(v̂+ε).
Calling AdaGrad's denominator a moving average. AdaGrad sums all past squared gradients; RMSProp uses a moving average.
Mixing β values: Adam β₂=0.999, RMSProp β=0.9. Using 0.999 in RMSProp makes it adapt very slowly.
Expecting Adam to always beat SGD. On some tasks well-tuned SGD with momentum generalizes better.

quiz.q: Write the AdaGrad update rule and state what G<sub>t</sub> accumulates.
quiz.a: G<sub>t</sub> = G<sub>t−1</sub> + g<sub>t</sub>²; w<sub>t+1</sub> = w<sub>t</sub> − η g<sub>t</sub>/(√G<sub>t</sub>+ε). G<sub>t</sub> accumulates the sum of squared gradients.

quiz.q: What are the standard Adam defaults for η, β₁, β₂, ε?
Why does RMSProp avoid AdaGrad's learning slowdown?
quiz.a: RMSProp uses a moving average of squared gradients, so old gradients decay and the denominator can shrink; AdaGrad's cumulative sum only grows.

quiz.q: What is bias correction in Adam and why is it needed?
quiz.a: Since m and v start at 0, early estimates are biased low. Dividing by 1−β₁^t and 1−β₂^t corrects this.

quiz.q: Run one Adam update for J=½w² from w=1 with η=0.1, β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, ε=10⁻⁸. Give w.
For AdaGrad with η=0.1, ε=0, starting w=1 on J=½w², compute w after two updates.
Compare the first step of RMSProp (β=0.9) and AdaGrad with η=0.1, ε=10⁻⁸ on J=½w² starting w=1. Which moves further and why?
quiz.a: RMSProp denominator √0.1≈0.316, step≈0.316; AdaGrad denominator≈1, step≈0.1. RMSProp moves further because its moving average gives less weight to the single squared gradient.

beyond: Not for the exam. AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive update and often improves generalization. Look up AMSGrad, AdaBelief and LAMB for large-batch training. In industry, Adam or AdamW is the default for transformers and CNNs, while SGD with momentum is still used for state-of-the-art image classification. Search 'AdamW decoupled weight decay' for the practical variant.
